title: Methodus nova et facilis calculum variationum tractandi

deep.reconstruction:
This page opens the 'Dilucidationes' (§§47–48) on curves with a maximum or minimum property, and it begins Euler's classification of such problems by the order of the resulting differential equation. Setting p=dy/dx, q=dp/dx, r=dq/dx, the problem is to make J=∫Z(x,y,p,q,r,...)dx stationary, with dZ = M dx + N dy + P dp + Q dq + R dr + .... The extremal curve then satisfies the (higher-order) Euler–Lagrange equation 0 = N − dP/dx + d²Q/dx² − d³R/dx³ + ...

Euler then makes a structural claim: unless P, Q, R vanish or are constant, this equation is always of even order (2nd, 4th, 6th, ...). It is never of 1st, 3rd, 5th or other odd order. He promises to explain this more clearly later.

§48 classifies problems by that order. The reason given is that the order fixes the number of arbitrary constants in the solution.
- Class I: the equation is finite (order 0).
- Class II: the equation is of second order.
- Class III: the equation is of fourth order, and so on.

The first case of Class I is Z=Z(x,y) only, so dZ = M dx + N dy. The extremal 'curve' is then the finite equation N = ∂Z/∂y = 0, which is pointwise optimisation with no free constants. The next page gives an example (Z=2xy−y², extremal y=x). It then extends Class I to Z+𝔷(x,y)p. Here the Euler–Lagrange equation reduces to Z_y − 𝔷_x = 0, because the 𝔷p part only re-expresses ∫𝔷 dy.

Modern reading: for a Lagrangian of order n that is regular in y^(n), the Euler–Lagrange equation has order 2n. Degenerate Lagrangians drop the order, but always by an even amount for a scalar unknown. The underlying reason is that the Fréchet derivative (linearisation) of an Euler–Lagrange expression is formally self-adjoint. A self-adjoint scalar linear differential operator has no odd-order leading term, since the adjoint of a·D^{2k+1} is −a·D^{2k+1} + lower-order terms. So Euler's parity claim is true in full generality for one dependent variable.
errors: The exception clause 'unless P, Q, R vanish or are constant' is imprecise. Order reduction occurs much more generally, e.g. whenever Z is affine in the highest derivative (Euler himself treats Z+𝔷p in §49). The correct statement is that the order is 2n for a regular Lagrangian and is reduced by even steps for degenerate ones. Euler's parity conclusion still survives.
No proof of the parity claim is given on this page; it is deferred ('mox clarius exponemus').

Neighbouring page (§48 example): for ∫(2xy−y²)dx, the extremal y=x gives the value x³/3 and Euler calls this smaller than for any other curve. But 2xy−y² = x² − (x−y)² ≤ x², so x³/3 is a maximum, not a minimum. 'minor' should be 'maior'.

ideas.what: Euler–Lagrange equation for Lagrangians depending on higher derivatives, 0 = N − dP/dx + d²Q/dx² − ...
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (Methodus inveniendi, 1744); the δ-method formulation is due to Lagrange (1760s)
ideas.where_published: E65 Methodus inveniendi lineas curvas (1744); E296 Elementa calculi variationum; E420 itself

ideas.what: The extremal equation of a single-function variational problem is always of even order (or finite), never of odd order
ideas.modern_name: Even-order property of scalar Euler–Lagrange equations; a consequence of the formal self-adjointness of the Fréchet derivative (Helmholtz conditions, inverse problem of the calculus of variations)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Folklore in the inverse-problem literature (Helmholtz 1887, Douglas 1941, modern expositions such as Olver); Euler's early explicit observation is rarely cited
ideas.where_published: Stated here in E420 §47; possibly implicit in E65's treatment of orders

ideas.what: Classification of variational problems by the order of the Euler–Lagrange equation, linked to the number of arbitrary constants; Class I gives finite equations N=0
ideas.modern_name: Order of extremal equations / degenerate Lagrangians (pointwise optimisation as the order-zero case)

missed.claim: Euler states as a general structural fact that variational problems in one unknown function never produce odd-order equations. This is exactly the scalar necessary condition (self-adjointness of the linearised operator) later formalised in the inverse problem of the calculus of variations. Together with §49 (Z+𝔷p giving finite equations, i.e. the role of exact/null-Lagrangian terms), it anticipates themes of the Helmholtz-condition and null-Lagrangian theory. Histories of the inverse problem generally do not cite Euler 1772 for the parity observation.
missed.quote: quod ista aequatio nunquam vel simpliciter differentialis, vel tertii, vel quinti, aliusue gradus imparis euadat
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Mainly historiographical: it gives Euler priority for an explicit statement of the odd-order obstruction to a variational formulation. The mathematics itself is well known today.

deep.surprise_reason: The content is the standard higher-order Euler–Lagrange equation plus a classification scheme. The parity remark is a correct and somewhat prescient structural observation, but it is well known in substance and probably seen by Euler scholars; it is only historiographically under-credited.
transcription_corrections: 'in-voluit' corresponds to 'inuoluit' (hyphenated across the line); otherwise the transcription matches the image.
